title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti's new moratorium and the fight over Michigan data center power

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.

Tonight we're zeroing in on Ypsilanti Township's unanimous vote yesterday to freeze major utility projects, a move aimed squarely at a proposed University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory data center.
That moratorium on electric infrastructure is the big development we're unpacking first, Graham, because it shows how local pushback is evolving beyond just zoning fights.
Exactly. Trustees passed it at their August 18 meeting to limit big power lines and substations, directly blocking grid connections for the project at Textile and Bridge roads.
Why does this one matter more than the others we've seen? What's the history here with the U-M and Los Alamos proposal?

The project has been in the works for a while as a research-focused hyperscale facility. Yesterday's vote builds on earlier concerns about massive infrastructure serving a site tied to national lab work.
Residents are worried about power demand straining the grid for everyone else, right? What happens to electric bills if something like this goes through without limits?
That's the core worry. A facility this size could pull enormous amounts of electricity, and without new lines or upgrades, nearby homes and farms might face higher rates or reliability issues.
And water use? These centers need cooling. How does that play into the farmland and town impacts we're hearing about across the state?
Water draw is a recurring flashpoint. In Ypsilanti's case, the moratorium gives the township time to review how any new infrastructure would affect local resources before anything is locked in.
Who are the main players pushing back here? Is it mostly residents, or are township officials leading the charge?
It was a unanimous board vote, so officials are aligned with resident concerns about losing local say over power routes that could cut through neighborhoods and fields.
What happens next? Does this moratorium stick, or could the project find another route around it?
The township will likely use the pause to draft stricter rules on utility projects. Similar moves in other areas suggest this could slow things down for months while reviews happen.
We've seen power-line bans in other spots too. How does this fit the bigger pattern of townships trying to hit the brakes?
It's part of a growing wave where communities are targeting the infrastructure first because that's what actually enables the buildout. It forces developers to negotiate or scale back.
And for listeners 30 or 60 miles away, why should they care about one township's vote?
Because power grids are connected. One big project without proper limits can ripple into rate increases or capacity issues for utilities serving a much wider area.
Fair point. Let's shift to today's other developments starting with the Saline area.

Right. The developer behind the large Saline Township campus bought the neighboring golf course today, which has residents concerned it signals plans for even bigger land use and more tax-break requests.
Local officials haven't commented yet on how this changes pending reviews. Does the purchase change the power demand picture?
It likely does. Expanding onto that extra land could mean higher overall electricity needs, which ties directly into the same grid strain worries we just discussed.
Next up, former congressman Mike Rogers spoke in Detroit today calling for a temporary halt on new data centers to avoid higher power costs.
Yes, he told voters that AI-driven demand is already pressuring utilities, and facilities 30 miles away could push bills up for residents if there's no pause.
That aligns with the rate concerns from the moratorium story. Any sense of how widespread those cost impacts could be?
It's the same theme: without caps or better planning, the load from multiple large projects adds up quickly across the state.
Another today story: a township passed a ban on new electrical infrastructure to stop a 220,000-square-foot U-M backed project tied to Los Alamos.
That one directly cuts off the grid connection for the hyperscale site, leaving residents and farms facing the prospect of major power lines without much local input.
Sounds like a more aggressive version of the Ypsilanti approach. How do these bans usually hold up legally?
They often lead to negotiations or court challenges, but they buy time for communities to write clearer rules first.
Also today, the OpenAI-Oracle developer bought a golf course next to their planned Michigan campus, signaling possible expansion despite pushback.
Nearby residents are now asking about noise, traffic, and exactly how much power the larger footprint would draw from the grid.
New Buffalo Township turned down a special land-use request for a data center on Kluver Road after hearing concerns about water and noise.
The denial keeps that project from moving forward for now in southwest Michigan.
Shifting to yesterday's items, Mundy Township in Genesee County is seeing early interest in a former manufacturing site for a potential data center.
Officials are fielding questions about water draw and grid upgrades, with residents concerned about property values and taxes.
Bay City neighbors packed a planning meeting yesterday to oppose proposed data centers over power, water, and industrial noise reaching homes.
The turnout shows how quickly these worries are spreading in mid-Michigan towns.
Mason residents also rejected a proposal yesterday, warning it would push local utilities past capacity and raise household rates.
Speakers questioned whether any promised tax revenue would cover the long-term costs to the community.
And St. Joseph County is weighing a year-long moratorium after similar alarms on power and water use.
That pause would give them time to write rules before projects lock in contracts, affecting how fast these facilities spread into rural counties.
Plenty of activity. Let's look ahead to tonight's meetings listeners might want to follow or attend.
Emmet County Board of Commissioners is considering a resolution to delay data center permits until March 2027.
Lodi Township Planning Commission Data Center Subcommittee meets to review zoning regulations and moratorium options.
There's also the Lodi Township Data Center Subcommittee discussing the ordinance and planning.
Somerset Township Board of Trustees has a regular meeting where a proposed data center moratorium ordinance could come up.
And Grass Lake Charter Township Planning Commission is meeting, with data center topics possibly on the agenda.
Good chances for public input in several spots tonight.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Moratorium Targets U-M Data Center Power Lines
